taxonomyNote: NatureServe lists the primary common name as Common Watersnake (Nerodia sipedon); same scientific name.
fieldMarks: Brownish, tan or gray; back and sides have square blotches alternating and often merging into bands toward the front; large adults can look solid brown or black, especially when dry.
Belly white, yellowish or orangish, with dark half-moon marks and often red or orange blotches.
Juveniles have reddish-brown saddles on a tan, brown or gray ground colour.
Scales keeled, anal plate divided, 21-25 scales at midbody; adults 61-140 cm, males smaller than females; mature males have knobbed keels near the vent.
behavior: Active day and night but mainly by day; basks on overhanging branches, beaver lodges, logs and shallow margins; social at basking sites in spring and fall, otherwise solitary.
Eats amphibians, fish (live or dead), crayfish, insects, leeches, small mammals; swallows prey alive and is not a constrictor.
Inactive in cold months in the north (activity mainly March-April through October); bites and discharges musk when handled.
habitat: Creeks, rivers, canals, lakes, ponds, marshes, bogs and swamps; favours sunny spots with debris, logs or rocks at the water's edge.
Hibernates in burrows, rock crevices or uplands near water.
range: Southern Ontario and the northeastern United States, from Nebraska and Kansas east to the Atlantic coast and south to North Carolina and southern Missouri.

lookalikes.name: Northern cottonmouth (water moccasin)
lookalikes.howToTell: Commonly mistaken for it; the northern water snake is non-venomous (Animal Diversity Web gives no further field mark).
